Elsewhere, Chapter 9 passes on a doctor's suggestion, "of course depending upon a doctor's advice" (<3>p. 133</3>), to keep chocolate on hand "for its quick energy value at times of fatigue" (<4>p. 134</4>), since a vague craving at night could be satisfied by candy (<5>p. 134</5>).
4706a9e06754: <0>Angry.</0> This is the one with the most weight. Resentment is the "number one" offender, and "It destroys more alcoholics than anything else." (<1>p. 64</1>). "If we were to live, we had to be free of anger." (<2>p. 66</2>). A wife's nagging about her husband's smoking and coffee threw him "into a fit of anger. He got drunk." (<3>p. 135</3>), and the book adds that he was "dead wrong" (<4>p. 135</4>). Chapter 10 names "The greatest enemies of us alcoholics" as "resentment, jealousy, envy, frustration, and fear" (<5>p. 145</5>). Chapter 3 also says that when they drank deliberately, feeling justified "by nervousness, anger, worry, depression, jealousy or the like," the justification was "insanely insufficient in the light of what always happened" (<6>p. 37</6>).
8902db29359c: <0>Lonely.</0> Bill's own story has loneliness leading to a drink, years before A.A.: sailing for the war, "I was very lonely and again turned to alcohol." (<1>p. 1</1>). After that, loneliness belongs to the drinking: Bill in "that bitter morass of self-pity" (<2>p. 8</2>), and "the chilling vapor that is loneliness" of the last days of drinking (<3>p. 151</3>). In the Akron hotel lobby, Bill thought that without a few drinks he might "have a lonely week-end" (<4>p. 154</4>); what he did was phone a clergyman to find another alcoholic (<5>p. 154</5>). Chapter 7 promises the helper the chance "to watch loneliness vanish" (<6>p. 89</6>).
76ef4c1df584: <0>Tired.</0> Step Eleven's practice of pausing through the day ends: "We do not tire so easily, for we are not burning up energy foolishly" (<1>p. 88</1>). Chapter 10 warns employers that a newly sober man "may overdo" and may need his sixteen-hour days curbed (<2>p. 146</2>). And there is the chocolate "at times of fatigue" (<3>p. 134</3>).
